clinicalScope: Epidemiology as a public‑health discipline applied to common diseases and health problems in East African and other low‑resource hospital settings
subject: Public health
summary: Epidemiology studies how diseases spread, who gets them, and why. In East African hospitals it guides clinicians to recognise patterns, target limited resources and prevent illness.

sections.p: Epidemiology is the systematic study of the distribution and determinants of health‑related states in populations, and the application of this knowledge to control health problems.
b: Descriptive: person, place, time
Analytical: risk‑factor identification
Applied: planning interventions
Focus on communicable, non‑communicable and injury‑related conditions

sections.p: In East Africa the leading causes of morbidity and mortality are infectious diseases (malaria, HIV, TB), perinatal conditions, and emerging non‑communicable diseases (hypertension, diabetes).
b: Malaria accounts for ~20% of outpatient visits in rural hospitals
HIV prevalence in adults 15‑49 y ranges 4‑7 % in most countries
TB incidence ≈ 200 per 100 000 population
Hypertension prevalence ≈ 25 % in urban adults

sections.p: Determinants are the social, economic, environmental and biological factors that shape disease patterns.
b: Poverty → limited access to clean water, nutrition, health care
Agricultural work → exposure to vector habitats (mosquitoes, tsetse)
Urbanisation → crowding, air pollution, sedentary lifestyle
Genetic predisposition (e.g., sickle‑cell trait) interacts with infections

sections.p: Surveillance collects routine data to detect trends, outbreaks and evaluate interventions. In low‑resource settings, simple tools (paper registers, mobile SMS) are often used.

t.b: Is transmission increasing? – Rising counts suggest outbreak; compare to seasonal baseline
What are preventable causes? – Identify delays in referral, hemorrhage, infection
Is the program effective? – <85 % indicates need for adherence support
What proportion is uncontrolled? – Guides community‑based hypertension program

sections.p: Screening aims to detect disease early when treatment is more effective; prevention reduces incidence.
b: Malaria: intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) and insecticide‑treated nets
HIV: provider‑initiated testing and counseling (PITC) in all admissions
Hypertension: opportunistic BP measurement at every clinic visit
Cervical cancer: visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) where cytology unavailable

sections.p: Implementation science evaluates how best to deliver evidence‑based interventions within existing health‑system constraints.
b: Task‑shifting: train community health workers to dispense antimalarials
Bundle care for obstetric hemorrhage (uterotonics, tranexamic acid, rapid transport)
Integrated NCD clinics: combine hypertension, diabetes and HIV follow‑up
Use of mHealth reminders for medication adherence

sections.p: Strong health systems provide the platform for epidemiologic actions; policies translate data into action.
b: Essential medicines list ensures availability of first‑line drugs
District health information system (DHIS2) aggregates routine data
National malaria strategic plan sets targets for net coverage and case management
Financing: community health insurance schemes improve access

sections.p: Equity means reducing health gaps between groups; community engagement ensures interventions are culturally acceptable.
b: Engage tribal leaders to promote bed‑net use
Gender‑sensitive outreach for antenatal care in pastoralist communities
Subsidised transport vouchers for remote patients
Participatory mapping of disease hotspots

sections.p: M&E tracks whether interventions achieve intended outcomes and informs course correction.
b: Process indicators: % of health facilities reporting weekly malaria data
Outcome indicators: reduction in under‑5 malaria admissions by 30 % in 2 years
Impact indicators: decline in age‑standardised mortality rate
Use of rapid assessment surveys when routine data are incomplete

sections.p: Clinicians use epidemiologic information at the bedside to shape differential diagnoses, ordering of investigations and empiric therapy.
b: High local malaria incidence → treat febrile patient with ACT pending test
TB hotspot → consider TB in chronic cough even with negative sputum if resources limited
Seasonal cholera surge → early rehydration and oral cholera vaccine campaigns
Rising hypertension prevalence → screen all adult admissions

sections.p: Low‑resource settings face data quality, diagnostic capacity and workforce challenges.
b: Incomplete registers → under‑reporting of deaths
Delayed laboratory confirmation (e.g., culture) → reliance on clinical algorithms
Staff turnover → loss of surveillance expertise
Limited internet connectivity → delayed data upload

sections.p: Examiners test ability to translate epidemiologic data into clinical decisions, public‑health planning and critical appraisal of surveillance systems.
b: Interpret a trend graph of malaria cases and suggest next step
Identify key risk factors for an outbreak of typhoid in a refugee camp
Design a simple surveillance tool for postpartum hemorrhage
Critique the use of a single‑site study to estimate national HIV prevalence

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden surge in deaths or severe illness clusters
Unexplained high fever (>38 °C) in >3 days with no response to standard therapy
Rapidly increasing respiratory distress in a ward during rainy season

faq.q: Why is epidemiology important for a bedside doctor?
faq.a: It tells you which diseases are most likely in your setting, guiding empiric treatment and appropriate investigations.

faq.q: What if laboratory tests are unavailable?
faq.a: Use syndromic algorithms based on local disease prevalence and clinical patterns, and document uncertainty for later confirmation.

faq.q: How often should surveillance data be reviewed?
faq.a: At minimum weekly for acute infections; monthly for chronic conditions; and quarterly for program evaluation.

exam: A 4‑year‑old presents with fever, cough and night sweats in a high‑TB district – which epidemiologic factor most strongly supports starting empiric TB therapy? — High local TB incidence and prolonged cough >2 weeks.
You notice a 30 % rise in malaria admissions over two weeks; what is the first public‑health action? — Verify data, then trigger an outbreak response (vector control, community net distribution).

A district hospital lacks culture facilities; a patient with sepsis is not improving on antimalarials – how do you decide on empiric antibiotics? — Apply local bacterial prevalence data (e.g., gram‑negative bacilli common in urinary sepsis) and use broad‑spectrum agents recommended by national guidelines.
During a cholera outbreak, what surveillance indicator best measures control success? — Decrease in proportion of acute watery diarrhoea cases testing positive for Vibrio cholerae.

Explain why task‑shifting to community health workers can improve malaria case management. — Increases access to rapid diagnostic tests and ACTs, reduces delays, and aligns with WHO recommendations for low‑resource settings.
A health‑facility audit shows 40 % of maternal deaths occur after referral; what determinant does this highlight? — Delays in transport and referral systems (health‑system factor).

How would you evaluate the impact of a new hypertension screening program after 12 months? — Compare baseline and follow‑up prevalence of uncontrolled BP, assess treatment initiation rates, and calculate reduction in stroke admissions.

What is the main limitation of using hospital‑based mortality data to estimate community disease burden? — Selection bias: only the most severe cases reach the hospital, under‑representing milder community cases.
In a refugee camp, you observe a spike in diarrhoea; which risk factor is most likely driving it? — Overcrowding and inadequate water‑sanitation facilities.
Describe one way to ensure equity when distributing insecticide‑treated nets. — Prioritise households without previous net ownership and vulnerable groups (pregnant women, children <5 y).
